Various theories have been proposed:
* Three possibilities from Babiniotis:
*: 1. Inherited from Byzantine Greek [Term?], from Albanian lule or lulediell (“sunflower”).
*: 2. From λειρίδιον (leirídion), λειλίδιον (leilídion), from Koine Greek λειρίον (leiríon, “lily”), from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion, “id”).
*: 3. From Ancient Greek *λίλιον (*lílion) (from Latin lilium (“lily”)) + -ούδι (-oúdi, diminutive).
* From Kriaras:
*: Possibly from *λίλιον (*lílion), from Latin lilium (“lily”).
Regardless, the first part of the word is from the same ultimate source as English lily.

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek τραπέζιν (trapézin), via Koine Greek from Ancient Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion, “small table”), diminutive of τράπεζα (trápeza, “a table”). This is conventionally taken to be from a (virtual?) *τετράπεζα (*tetrápeza, “four-footed”), from τετράς (tetrás, “four”) and πέζα (péza, “-footed, -legged”), from πούς (poús, “a foot”). Sihler (1995) instead relates the first element to τρεῖς (treîs, “three”), noting that early tables had three legs, not four. Compare English trapeze, trapezium, trapezophoron. Doublet of τραπέζιον (trapézion), a borrowing.

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek νερό(ν) (neró(n)), from Koine Greek νηρόν (nērón), from νηρός (nērós, “wet, damp”), from Ancient Greek νεαρός (nearós, “young, fresh”), from the term νεαρὸν ὕδωρ (nearòn húdōr, “fresh water”). Cognate with Italiot Greek nerò, Pontic Greek νερόν (nerón). Displaced earlier Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr) almost entirely, except in compound terms and formal language. Sometimes misattributed to unrelated Etruscan 𐌍𐌄𐌓𐌉 (neri, “water”) or even Sanskrit नीर (nīra, “water”).

etymology_text:
From Hellenistic Koine Greek γάδαρος (gádaros) of 2nd century CE. Medieval γάιδαρος (gáidaros)/γάδαρος (gádaros)/γαΐδαρος (gaḯdaros) or γαϊδάριον (gaïdárion)
Origin theories:
* Uncertain, obscure: from Arabic غَيْذَار (ḡayḏār) with proposed meaning “harshness, oppression”.
* Based on the form γαύδαρος (gávdaros), the same word as Arabic كَوْدَن (kawdan, “beast of burden, particularly a mule or hinny”), which see for more, a word then also present in Khotanese [script needed] (khaḍara, “mule”), alleged source of Turkish katır (“mule”), Kazakh қашыр (qašır, “mule”) etc.
* Or from Hindi ghádar, gadarō or gadaró meaning “gypsy”.
* Not from γαϊδούρι (gaïdoúri) < (καρ)γαδούρι ((kar)gadoúri) from cargatore (literally “carrier”) from cargar (“to load onto oneself”)
* Not from the Ancient Greek γάδος (gádos, “cod”), common name: γαϊδουρόψαρο (gaïdourópsaro).

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek πεταλούδα (petaloúda), of uncertain further origin. Probably from an earlier unattested *πεταλίδα (*petalída) with change of suffix to -ούδα (-oúda), from the root underlying Ancient Greek πέτᾰλον (pétălon, “leaf, petal”) + -ίδα (-ída), with possible influence from the marginally-attested πετηλίς (petilís, “locust”). Alternatively, from Ancient Greek πετάννυμι (petánnumi, “to spread out, open”), which stems from the same Indo-European root as πέτᾰλον (pétălon) above.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek γάτα (gáta), an 11th-century parallel form of κάττα (kátta), from Medieval Latin gatta, from Late Latin catta.
Or, from Hellenistic κάττα (kátta) with sound change from liaison with the accusative of the feminine article τήν (tḗn) /tin ˈkata > tiŋˈɡata > ti ˈɣata/.
The mediaeval or Hellenistic form κάττα (kátta) and the simplified spelling κάτα (káta) survives in modern form κάτα (káta), diminutives (as κατσούλα (katsoúla)), dialectal and regional. From Late Latin catta. Also see the masculine γάτος (gátos), from Late Latin cattus.

Back-formation from the plural αβγά (avgá), itself extracted from ταβγά (tavgá, “the eggs”), a regular phonological development of Ancient Greek τά ᾠά (tá ōiá):

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm via Proto-Hellenic *ōyyón.

From Byzantine Greek κουτάλιν (koutálin), from Koine Greek κουτάλιον (koutálion) and κωτάλιον (kōtálion), diminutives of Koine Greek κώταλις (kṓtalis, “ladle, stirrer”), of unclear origin. Cognate with Pontic Greek κουτάλιν (koutálin), κουτάλι (koutáli), κουτάλ’ (koutál’).

etymology_text: Learned borrowing from Byzantine Greek δικήγορος (dikḗgoros), from late Hellenistic / Koine Greek, or medieval 6th century attested oblique cases (e.g. genitive δικηγόρου (dikēgórou), dative, δικηγόρῳ (dikēgórōi)), both suitable for a noun in -ήγορος or -ηγόρος, from Ancient Greek δίκη (díkē, “custom, law, judgment”) + -ήγορος (-ḗgoros), the latter suffix from ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to proclaim (in an assembly)”) with ectasis of <α> to <η> in composition (like κατήγορος (katḗgoros, “accuser”)), but with stress shift like δημηγόρος (dēmēgóros, “orator, speaker”). The word was lemmatized by Eustathius and at Suda as δικηγόρος (dikēgóros, “advocate”). Diccionario Español correctly lemmatizes δικηγόρος, unlike LSJ which lemmatizes δικήγορος.

etymology_text: Inherited from Byzantine Greek λάσπη (láspē), of unclear origin. ψωρο- (psoro-, “poor-”, from ψώρα "scabies" or "mange") + Κώσταινα (Kóstaina, feminine suffix for "wife of Kώστας"), see Κωνσταντίνος (Konstantínos).

: Patrick Leigh Fermor likens the name to the English "Mangy Betty" (see quotation below.)

etymology_text: From Koine Greek κανθόχοιρος (kanthókhoiros), from Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros), from ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “acanthus, a prickly plant”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”). Doublet of ακανθόχοιρος (akanthóchoiros).

examples.text:
1904, Folktale from Thrace in Nikolaos G. Polites, Studies of the life and languages of the Greek people, vol. 2, part 1, page 193.
Μία μάννα εἶχε τέσσερα παιδιά, τὸν σκαντζόχοιρο, τὴν ἀράχνη, τὴ χελῶνα καὶ τὴ μέλισσα. Ἦρθε καιρός καὶ ἀρρώστησε καὶ ἔστειλε νὰ φωνάξῃ τὸν σκαντζόχοιρο […]. Ό σκαντζόχοιρος ὅμως εἶπε […] πῶς ἔχει νὰ βάλῃ φράχταις ’ς τἀμπέλι του καὶ δὲν ἔχει καιρό. Ἡ μάννα του τὸν καταράστη τότε· «Νὰ του καθήσουν οἱ τσαλιαίς ’ς τὴ ῥάχη».
Mía mánna eíche téssera paidiá, ton skantzóchoiro, tin aráchni, ti chelóna kai ti mélissa. Írthe kairós kai arróstise kai ésteile na fonáxei ton skantzóchoiro […]. O skantzóchoiros ómos eípe […] pos échei na válei fráchtes 's tampéli tou kai den échei kairó. I mánna tou ton katarásti tóte; «Na tou kathísoun oi tsaliés 's ti ráchi».
examples.english: A mother had four children, a hedgehog, a spider, a turtle and a bee. There came a time when she got sick and she summoned the hedgehog […]. But the hedgehog said […] that he had to put fences at his vineyard and had no time. Then, his mother cursed him: "May the thorns [of the stakes for the fence] sit on his back."

etymology_text:
Via Byzantine Greek Ἀτσίγγανος (Atsínganos) and Ἀθίγγανος (Athínganos) from Ancient Greek ἀθίγγανος (athínganos, “who doesn't want to be touched; untouchable”), ultimately a compound of privative ἀ- (a-) + θιγγάνω (thingánō, “to touch”). The Middle Greek word had initially been the name of a Christian sect, the Melchizedekian sect, which was subsequently associated to Romani people.
Nişanyan suggests, due to the very recent first attestation of the term in Greek (1378 AD), Proto-Turkic *čï̄gań (“poor”) as its origin, which was already attested in the Bilge Qaghan inscriptions dated to 735, which, in turn, explains the replacement of the accent. This modern accent could also be influenced by the feminine form Ἀτσιγγάνα (Atsingána).
Petrounias, however, explains αθίγγανος (athínganos) as a paretymological variant of ἀτσίγγανος (atsínganos), influenced by the name of the Christian sect.
Also see Italian zingano, German Zigeuner, Turkish çingene.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek κουνουπίδιν (kounoupídin) (12th century), probably from a noun *κανωπίδιον (*kanōpídion), diminutive of Hellenistic κάνωπον (kánōpon, “a kind of short tree or bush”). See city of Κάνωπος (Kánōpos).
Also see the dialectal synonym καρναπίδι (karnapídi) / καρναμπίκι (karnampíki) / καρναμπίτι (karnampíti), ultimately from κράμβη (krámbē) with influence from (Ottoman) Turkish, as well as Albanian kunipidhë, from Ottoman Turkish قرنابیت (karnabit), قنبیط (kunnebit), from Arabic قَرْنَبِيط (qarnabīṭ), قُنَّبِيط (qunnabīṭ), itself from Ancient Greek κραμβίδιον (krambídion), a diminutive of κράμβη (krámbē). Doublet of καρναμπίτι (karnampíti).

etymology_text:
Back-formation from the plural αφτιά (aftiá), extracted from article & noun τ’ αφτιά (t’ aftiá, “the ears”), from Byzantine Greek τά ἀφτία (tá aphtía) (singular τό ἀφτίον (tó aphtíon)), from Koine Greek τά ὠτία (tá ōtía) (singular ὠτίον (ōtíon)), diminutive of Ancient Greek τᾰ̀ ὦτᾰ (tằ ôtă) (singular οὖς (oûs)), through a regular phonological development of
: /ta.uˈti.a/ → (*/tavˈti.a/) → /tafˈti.a/ and αφτιά (aftiá) /aˈftça/, singular αφτί (aftí) /aˈfti/.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws.
Etymology according to Georgios Hatzidakis, accepted by Babiniotis. Other linguists support the spelling αυτί (aftí) from τ’ αυτιά (t’ aftiá) through /tawˈti.a/ - /tafˈti.a/. Similar case is the spelling of αβγό (avgó) or αυγό (avgó, “egg”).

etymology_text:
Uncertain. Has been claimed to have been borrowed from Ottoman Turkish جبره (cibre, “grape pomace”), although according to different sources the borrowing occurred the other way round.
Alternatively, a relation to Ancient Greek σίκερα n (síkera, “a strong fermented drink”), which is from Biblical Hebrew שֵׁכָר m (šēḵār, “alcoholic drink”), has also been suggested.
Unrelated to the superficially similar τσιπούρα f (tsipoúra, “gilt-head bream, Sparus aurata”).

Our youth is going,
Our youth and coolness,
Our youth is going and vanishing,
And with it, our carefree times.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek ψέμα (pséma), from Hellenistic Koine Greek ψεῦμα (pseûma) with simplification [vm] > [m]. The expected double [mm] (ψέμμα) has not been written in mediaeval times because the simplification happened after the period when double consonants were pronounced -as in ῥεῦμα (rheûma) > ρέμα (réma). From Ancient Greek ψεῦσμα (pseûsma), a derivative of Ancient Greek ψεύδω (pseúdō) with suffix -μα (-ma).
Cognate with Mariupol Greek псе́ма (psjéma).

etymology_text:
From Ancient Greek πτηνός (ptēnós, “flying, winged creature, bird”), from πέτομαι (pétomai), itself from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti (“to fly”) from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).
 Beware Slavic false cognates such as Bulgarian пти́ца (ptíca), Macedonian птица (ptica), Russian пти́ца (ptíca), Serbo-Croatian пти̏ца/ptȉca, Ukrainian пти́ця (ptýcja), all meaning bird from Proto-Slavic *pъtica. True cognates are Old English feþer (English feather), Latin petō, Russian перо́ (peró), Sanskrit पतति (pátati), Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬙𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (pataⁱti), Old Armenian թիռ (tʻiṙ).

examples.ref: 1972, “Άλλος Για Χίο Τράβηξε [One Of Them Went And Left For Chios]”, in Manos Eleutheriou (lyrics), Dimos Moutsis (music), Άγιος Φεβρουάριος [Holy February], performed by Dimitris Mitropanos:

In wet, cobblestoned roads you spend the night,

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek μοῦχλα (moûkhla, “mould”), borrowed from (Western?) Aramaic מוּגְלָא / ܡܘܓܠܐ (muḡlā) (“pus, water under a blister”; in the usually attested Eastern language forms instead not actually recorded as “mould”, apparently then transferred from an idea of “damaging liquid”), when also around the same time Middle Armenian forms the compound մգլահոտ (mglahot, “smelling like mould; smell of mould”), as otherwise the present term would have to be from Ancient Greek ὀμίχλη (omíkhlē, “mist, fog; vapour; obscurity”) and the Armenian term մգլել (mglel, “to mould”) parallelly from մէգ (mēg, “mist”); prompt to conjecture native etymologies, Indo-Europeanists sport the leading opinion even that the Bulgarian and Macedonian terms in the descendants section below would rather hail from Proto-Slavic *mъxъ (“moss”) + *-ъlъ.

etymology_text:
Borrowed.
* Either a learned borrowing from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) (according to Andriotis).
* Or from Ottoman Turkish خلیفه (halife), from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) (according to Babiniotis). From the Arabic, also derived the Mediaeval Greek χαλιφᾶς (khaliphâs, “Muhammad's successor”) of the 11th century, with a later sense "Muslim political and religious leader".
* Or a learned borrowing from Italian califfo or French calife (according to Petrounias), stem [kalif-] + ending -ης, from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) with [k > x] under the influence of the Mediaeval χαλιφᾶς (khaliphâs).

—Zorba … We'll eat and drink together, and then, you'll play the santouri

args.note0: Older or formal genitive singular: παραδόσεως (paradóseos)

etymology_text:
Learnedly, from Ancient Greek παράδοσις (parádosis) + modern ending -ση (-si), thus παρά- (pará-) + δόση f (dósi, “dose, portion, gift”).
The Triantafyllidis Dictionary suggests that the sense of "tradition" is influenced by semantic loan from French tradition and German Überlieferung, which are themselves from traditio, which in had its sense of "tradition" ("saying or teaching handed down generationally, especially ecclesiastical tradition") influenced by the Koine Greek παράδοσις (parádosis)

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek κουτσός (koutsós), of uncertain etymology. Likely from Middle Bulgarian коуцъ (kucŭ, “lame, crippled”), from Proto-Slavic *kucъ (“crippled, tailless”), of expressive origin. Another possibility is derivation from late Koine Greek κοξός (koxós, “lame”), borrowed from Late Latin coxus (“lame, crippled”), from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *koḱs-.

etymology_text:
From κουτουρού (koutouroú).
2 Possibilities exist:
* From either Ottoman Turkish كوتردی (kütürdü, kütürtü) or كوتور (kütür) both with the meaning related to a crashing or cracking or hard hitting sound from كوت (küt) or كوت كوت (küt küt) which are likely onomatopoeic. The semantic shift from a type of hard sound to stupidity or foolishness is unexplained and is likely a Greek innovation.
* From Ottoman Turkish كوتورم (kötürüm, “paralyzed, crippled, bedridden”). The semantic shift here is more viable but the missing final consonant /m/ is less explainable.

etymology_text: Exact calque of French billion, with the wrong bi- (“bi-, twice”) corresponding to δίς (dís, “twice, two”) and million to εκατομμύριο (ekatommýrio, “hundred myriad, million”). Thus literally "two million". The mathematically correct formation would be χίλια (chília, “a thousand”) + εκατομμύριο (ekatommýrio). Attested in 1871. Compare to the ancient δισχίλιος (diskhílios, “two thousand”) and δισμύριος (dismúrios, “twenty thousand (twice ten thousand)”).

1935 - George Seferis, Μυθιστόρημα ΚΓ´, [Mythistorema] (poems), 23. 1935, Original polytonic spelling. At George Seferis: Collected Poems, 1924-1955. Bilingual Edition pp56-57.
Λίγο ἀκόμα
θὰ ἰδοῦμε τὶς ἀμυγδαλιὲς ν’ ἀνθίζουν
τὰ μάρμαρα νὰ λάμπουν στὸν ἥλιο
τὴ θάλασσα νὰ κυματίζει
λίγο ἀκόμα,
νὰ σηκωθοῦμε λίγο ψηλότερα.
Lígo akóma
thá idoúme tís amygdaliés n’ anthízoun
tá mármara ná lámpoun stón ílio
tí thálassa ná kymatízei
lígo akóma,
ná sikothoúme lígo psilótera.
A little farther
we will see the almond trees blossoming
the marble gleaming in the sun
the sea breaking into waves
a little farther,
let us rise a little higher.

examples.english: Instead of just telling me he didn't want to come, he told me that he had something he had to do; excuses, excuses...

examples.text: Αυτός είναι διευθυντής εδώ και τριάντα χρόνια και δεν πρόκειται να παραιτηθεί· είναι καρεκλοκένταυρος.

examples.text: Ήμουν μόνη και στο συμβούλιο των αποφάσεων συμμετείχαν δώδεκα καρεκλοκένταυροι. Όταν δε πληροφορήθηκα πως το νέο κτίριο ήταν συμφερόντων του Ιδρύματος Νοταρά, ήτοι του μεγαλοεργολάβου Χανδρά, κατάλαβα πολλά.

examples.english: I was alone and there were twelve bureaucrats taking part in the decisive council. When I wasn't informed that the new building wasn't in the Notara Institute's interests, that is to say of the great engineer Chandras, I understood well.
examples.roman: Ímoun móni kai sto symvoúlio ton apofáseon symmeteíchan dódeka kareklokéntavroi. Ótan de pliroforíthika pos to néo ktírio ítan symferónton tou Idrýmatos Notará, ítoi tou megaloergolávou Chandrá, katálava pollá.

examples.ref: 2011, Το κορίτσι του διπλανού portal κυκλοφορεί και απορεί, →ISBN:
examples.english: The Cavalier tells you that he rented young girls by the dozen in Italy, aren't we entitled to a lightly matured one, we are! But not to have her ridiculed in the public sphere by that player!
examples.roman: Edó sou léei o kavaliére tis místhone me tin ntouzína tis anílikes stin Italía, den dikaioúmetha ki emeís mía elafrós siteméni, Dikaioúmetha! Óchi ómos kai na ti rezilépsei ston koinonikó tis perígyro o péftoulas!
examples.translation: The Cavalier tells you that he rented young girls by the dozen in Italy, aren't we entitled to a lightly matured one, we are! But not to have her ridiculed in the public sphere by that player!

examples.text: Έτσι ο Περσέας μεγάλωσε στη Σέριφο και θέριεψε κι έγινε παλίκαρος απ’ τους λίγους, αλλά του Πολυδέκτη, που βασίλευε στη γραφική νήσο κι έπαιρνε τρελές μίζες για να πουλάει προστασία στις ταβέρνες και γενικώς ήτανε σάπιος πέφτουλας […]
examples.ref: 2016, Αύγουστος Κορτώ, Νεοελληνική Μυθολογία, →ISBN:
examples.english: And so Perseus grew up in Serifos and grew wild and became a strapping young man – one of few – but Polydectes, who ruled on the picturesque island, took crazy bribes in order to sell protection to the taverns and generally was a rotten player.
examples.roman: Étsi o Perséas megálose sti Sérifo kai thériepse ki égine palíkaros ap’ tous lígous, allá tou Polydékti, pou vasíleve sti grafikí níso ki épairne trelés mízes gia na pouláei prostasía stis tavérnes kai genikós ítane sápios péftoulas […]
examples.translation: And so Perseus grew up in Serifos and grew wild and became a strapping young man – one of few – but Polydectes, who ruled on the picturesque island, took crazy bribes in order to sell protection to the taverns and generally was a rotten player.

etymology_text:
Οf uncertain etymon, with multiple theories proposed. Medieval spelling as in Τσακωνία f (Tsakonía, “area of Tsakonia”), or as in τζακονικός.
* Ahrweiler associates the ethnonym of the inhabitants of Τσακωνία (Tsakonía, “Tsakonia”) with the medieval parallel use for the sense "guardians", or "soldiers" Tσάκωνες, Τζάκωνες, Τζέκωνες (or -ονες) from the words ζάκα, σάκα (military guard), of Arabic, Semitic origin (see Greek σάκκος (sákkos), Classical Syriac ܣܩܐ,), to τζάκων, τσάκων.
* From the plural διάκονες or διάκονοι of the mediaeval διάκων (diákōn) or the ancient δῐᾱ́κονος (dĭā́konos, “servant, deacon of Christian church”), with mediaeval regional sense: "guardians", or "soldiers".. In this case, an etymologically informed spelling would be Τσάκονας with omicron.
*: The spelling with omega Τσάκωνας has prevailed, regardless of etymological concerns.
* From *Ἐξω-Λάκωνες (Exō-Lákōnes, “Outer-Laconians”) with a change of [ks] to [ts], typical of Tsakonian, and omission of [l]
Not likely:
* From τρᾱχών (trākhṓn, “rugged, stony tract”) genitive: τρᾱχῶνος; see τραχύς (trakhús, “jagged”).
* From Albanian tsakon (“rough, rugged land”)
* From phrase εἰς τούς Λάκωνας (eis toús Lákōnas, “to the Laconians”).
* From Slavic roots

glosses: Tsakonian: of or relating to the people of the Tsakonia area

etymology_text: Of late 18th–early 19th c. as a neologism from άλευρον (álevron, “flour”) + γαία (gaía, “earth”), in reference to the flour-like consistency of this alkaline earth oxide. etymology_text: Inherited from Byzantine Greek τσαγκάρης (tsankárēs), from Mediaeval and Late Koine Greek τσαγκάριος (tsankários) & τζαγκάριος (tzankários), τζαγγάριος (tzangários) with simplification of ⟨γγ > γκ⟩, from Koine Greek τζάγγη (tzángē) + -άριος (-ários). The Hellenistic term, chiefly in the plural, found as a transcription of Late Latin zancha / tzanga, from Persian ظانگا (zângâ) as in Parthian. Cognates include the Byzantine Greek τζαγγίον n (tzangíon, “a kind of Byzantine shoe”) and possibly the modern τσαγανό n (tsaganó). Compare Italian zingaro (“Gypsy”).

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek ξεφτέριν (xephtérin) < ξυπτέριν < ἐξυπτέριον, from Koine Greek ὀξυπτέριον n (oxuptérion, “hawk”) with assimilation of pronunciation [pt] > [ft] and with the influence of ξε- (xe-). a diminutive of Ancient Greek ὀξύπτερος (oxúpteros, “sharp-winged, hence swift-winged”) < ὀξύς (oxús) + πτερ(όν) n (pter(ón), “wing”) + -ος (-os). Compare to ὠκύπτερος (ōkúpteros, “swift-winged”) and the etymologies of ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp”) and ὠκύς (ōkús, “quick”).
Cognate with Pontic Greek ξυφτέριν (xyftérin) and akin to τσίφτης (tsíftis) and Albanian qift. Probably, not related to the Latin accipiter from acus.

args.note0: Older or formal genitive singular: ωριμάνσεως (orimánseos)
args.note: Also check ωρίμαση.

etymology_text:
Learned borrowing from Katharevousa ὡρίμανσις (orímansis), already attested in 1881 and proscribed by Koumanoudis with ironic comments, (also at other dictionaries) because of its formation from nonexistent verb *ὡριμαίνω, instead of the expected form ὡρίμασις (orímasis) (attested since 1796) -modern ωρίμαση (orímasi)-.
Created with Koine Greek ὡριμάζω (hōrimázō), modern ωριμά(ζω) (orimá(zo)) + feminine ending -ση (-si) with presence of ⟨-ν (n)-⟩ > -ν-ση as a hypercorrection to sound 'more ancient' according to the ancient pattern γηράσκω (girásko) > γήρανσις (gḗransis) as though from *γηραίνω, itself according to ὑγιαίνω (hugiaínō), past stem ὑγιαν- > ὑγίανσις (hugíansis), also ὑγίασις (hugíasis).
notes: The ending -νση is expected from verbs in -αίνω or -ύνω, with the nu ⟨-ν-⟩ present in their stems. Still, the form ωρίμανση is most popular.

glosses: ripening, maturing and see senses at verb ωριμάζω (orimázo)

examples.text: Τα μεθυσμένα σ’ αγαπώ / Ενός λεπτού είναι συμβάντα / Εγώ μια μέρα θα στα πω / Και θα κρατήσουνε για πάντα.
examples.ref: 1994, “Τα μεθυσμένα σ’ αγαπώ”, in Ελένη Γιαννατσούλια (lyrics), Phoebus (music), Πες αυτό που θέλεις, performed by Angela Dimitriou:
examples.english: The drunk "I love you"s / Are one-minute events / One day I will say them to you / And will last for ever.
examples.roman: Ta methysména s’ agapó / Enós leptoú eínai symvánta / Egó mia méra tha sta po / Kai tha kratísoune gia pánta.
examples.translation: The drunk "I love you"s / Are one-minute events / One day I will say them to you / And will last for ever.

examples.text: πόσες χιλιάδες σ’ αγαπώ / ερωτευμένα θα σού πώ
examples.ref: 2012, “Πόσα χιλιάδες καλοκαίρια”, in Νίκος Μωραΐτης (lyrics), DEMY #1, performed by Demy:
examples.english: How many thousands "I love you"'s / being in love I will tell you.
examples.roman: póses chiliádes s’ agapó / erotevména tha soú pó
examples.translation: How many thousands "I love you"'s / being in love I will tell you.

examples.text: Τα πιο μεγάλα σ’ αγαπώ τα λένε οι ψεύτες, / αυτοί που τάζουνε και φεύγουνε σαν κλέφτες. / Το σ’ αγαπώ δε θα τ’ ακούς από εμένα
examples.ref: 2018, “Τα πιο μεγάλα σ' αγαπώ”, in Στέλιος Μαργωμένος (lyrics), ...και ο έρως θεός είναι, performed by Notis Sfakianakis:
examples.english: Liars say the biggest "I love you"'s / those who promise and leave like thieves. / You won't hear the "I love you" from me.
examples.roman: Ta pio megála s’ agapó ta léne oi pséftes, / aftoí pou tázoune kai févgoune san kléftes. / To s’ agapó de tha t’ akoús apó eména

etymology_text: Unknown. Possibly from Byzantine Greek βήσσαλον (bḗssalon), from Late Latin bessalis (“small brick, tile”). Alternatively, has been interpreted as deriving from Italian bozzolo (“cocoon”), although this interpretation remains generally unsupported by most linguists due to semantic and phonological challenges. Another possibility is that it derives from Ancient Greek βολάχι (bolákhi), itself a diminutive form of βόλος (bólos). The affrication of the phoneme /k/ before the front vowel /i/ may have transformed βολάχι (bolákhi) to *βολάτσι (*bolátsi) and eventually βότσαλο (bótsalo). This etymology may be attested in γιαλόβολος (gialóvolos) and γιαλόβουλος (gialóvoulos), both meaning "sea-pebble."

glosses: small stone rounded and eroded by a body of water; pebble

etymology_text:
Of unclear origin. One theory derives the word from κουτσούπι (koutsoúpi, “tree trunk”) + -ιά (-iá) (as the Judas tree's flowers tend to blossom very close to its trunk), the former of apparently disputed origin:
* From Byzantine Greek κουζοῦπες (kouzoûpes), perhaps borrowed from Arabic [Term?].
* Related to κούτσουρο (koútsouro, “tree trunk, heavy object”), itself from Byzantine Greek κούτσουρον (koútsouron), neuter of κούτσουρος (koútsouros), of uncertain origin:
** From κουτσός (koutsós, “crippled, broken”) + ουρά (ourá, “tail”).
** From an unattested *κόψουρον (*kópsouron, “with a cut tail”), from the past stem *κοψ- (*kops-) of κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut, strike”) + ουρά (ourá, “tail”).

etymology_text:
Nominal formation probably cognate with, though apparently not derived from, Ancient Greek σήθω (sḗthō, “to sieve, sift”) (which would render a modern neuter noun *σήστρο; compare Hesychius' plural σῆστρα n (sêstra) of σῆστρον (sêstron)) under folk-etymological influence of the ancient σητάνιος / σητάνειος (sētánios / sētáneios, “of this year; this year's sieved wheat”), a form surviving in some modern Greek dialects, as the South Italiot Greek.
Τhe theory taking the word as borrowed from Slavic (Proto-Slavic *sìto (“sieve”)) is considered improbable.

glosses: sieve (a tool with a fine mesh used to sift flour, sand, etc.)
window screen (a mesh set in a frame used to keep foreign debris and insects out of a room without blocking fresh airflow)

etymology_text: Borrowed from Turkish pancur, panjur + -ι (-i). Nishanyan derives the Turkish from a French pare-jour (“light-organizing; lattice cage”, literally “adorn-daylight”); however, the French term apparently lacks attestation in texts, in addition to the term bearing strong resemblance to Persian پَنْجَرِه (panjere, “window, lattice”) (which was borrowed into Ottoman Turkish as پنجره (pencere)). Other theories consider the Turkish as borrowed from French abat-jour (“lampshade”) (which was borrowed into Greek as αμπαζούρ (ampazoúr)); however, this is phonetically less likely.

examples.ref: 2023 February 18, “«Αποφεύξιμη» η εντατική χρήση επικίνδυνων φυτοφαρμάκων από τους Ιταλούς μηλοπαραγωγούς”, in ypaithros.gr, archived from the original on 30 Mar 2023:
examples.english: "In addition to the risks to human health, almost a quarter of the pesticides used are believed to be particularly harmful to beneficial insects such as ichneumonids," notes Christine Vogt, one of the authors of the report.
examples.roman: «Ektós apó tous kindýnous gia tin anthrópini ygeía, schedón to 1/4 ton fytofarmákon pou chrisimopoioúntai pistévetai óti eínai idiaítera epivlavés gia ofélima éntoma ópos oi ichnevmonídes», episimaínei i Christine Vogt, mía apó tis syntáktries tis ékthesis.
examples.translation: "In addition to the risks to human health, almost a quarter of the pesticides used are believed to be particularly harmful to beneficial insects such as ichneumonids," notes Christine Vogt, one of the authors of the report.

examples.text: Μόλις το έκανε αυτό, συνειδητοποίησε ότι ανήκει στο είδος των τεττιγονίδων.
examples.ref: 2017 May 5, Newsroom, “Είδε ένα παράξενο Έντομο στην Αυλή του και Προσπάθησε να το πιάσει. Μόλις δείτε ΤΙ κάνει το έντομο, θα Χάσετε το Μυαλό σας!”, in Fanpage, archived from the original on 14 Oct 2024:
examples.english: As soon as he did this, he realized that it was a species of the Tettigoniidae.
examples.roman: Mólis to ékane aftó, syneiditopoíise óti aníkei sto eídos ton tettigonídon.
examples.translation: As soon as he did this, he realized that it was a species of the Tettigoniidae.

examples.text: Στις τεττιγονίδες, (Tettigonidae^([sic])) είναι σημαντικό το σχήμα του ωοαποθετήρα στα θηλυκά (εικ. 9-10), όπως επίσης και η διαμόρφωση της κάτω πλευράς του τελευταίου τμήματος της κοιλιάς (εικ. 11).
examples.ref: 2018 September 27, Luc Willemse, R. M. J. C. Kleukers, Baudewijn Odé, translated by Vassiliki I. Kati, Κλείδα αναγνώρισης των Ορθοπτέρων της Ελλάδας [The grasshoppers of Greece.], page 2:
examples.english: In the tettigoniids, (Tettigonidae^([sic])) the shape of the ovipositor in females is important (fig. 9-10), as is the configuration of the underside of the last segment of the abdomen (fig. 11).
examples.roman: Stis tettigonídes, (Tettigonidae^([sic])) eínai simantikó to schíma tou ooapothetíra sta thilyká (eik. 9-10), ópos epísis kai i diamórfosi tis káto plevrás tou teleftaíou tmímatos tis koiliás (eik. 11).
examples.translation: In the tettigoniids, (Tettigonidae^([sic])) the shape of the ovipositor in females is important (fig. 9-10), as is the configuration of the underside of the last segment of the abdomen (fig. 11).

examples.text: Τα έντομα αυτά δεν είναι αληθινοί γρύλοι, αλλά είναι «μακρυκεράτιες ακρίδες», ονόματι τεττιγονίδες.
examples.ref: 2023 June 19, Alfavita Newsroom, “Απίστευτες εικόνες! Ο απόλυτος εφιάλτης με "απόκοσμα" έντομα να μαστίζουν μια περιοχή!”, in Alfavita, archived from the original on 19 Jun 2023:
examples.english: These insects are not true crickets, but are "long-horned grasshoppers," called tettigoniids.
examples.roman: Ta éntoma aftá den eínai alithinoí grýloi, allá eínai «makrykeráties akrídes», onómati tettigonídes.
examples.translation: These insects are not true crickets, but are "long-horned grasshoppers," called tettigoniids.

examples.text: Τζιτζίκι είναι το λαϊκό όνομα διάφορων ειδών εντόμων από την οικογένεια Κικαδίδες (Cicadidae).
examples.ref: 2018 July 9, kgrek, “Περί τζιτζικιών και όχι μόνο..”, in ΜΠΟΡΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΘΑ ΠΕΡΑΣΕΙ - Let's wait until the storm passes, archived from the original on 28 Apr 2025:
examples.english: Cicada is the popular name for various species of insects from the family Cicadidae (Cicadidae).
examples.roman: Tzitzíki eínai to laïkó ónoma diáforon eidón entómon apó tin oikogéneia Kikadídes (Cicadidae).
examples.translation: Cicada is the popular name for various species of insects from the family Cicadidae (Cicadidae).

examples.text: Σε παλιότερα ταξινομικά συστήματα όλα τα συγγενικά είδη ονομάζονταν Τετιγίδες ή Κικαδίδες (Cicadidae), από το ελληνικό ή το λατινικό ηχομιμητικό όνομα των τζιτζικιών.
examples.ref: 2021 June 6, Μάρθα Χριστοφόγλου, “Μάρθα Χριστοφόγλου: Με αφορμή τα τζιτζίκια”, in Περιοδικό Περί Ου, archived from the original on 02 Nov 2024:
examples.english: In older taxonomic systems, all related species were called tettigids or cicadids (Cicadidae), from the Greek or Latin onomatopoeic name for cicadas.
examples.roman: Se paliótera taxinomiká systímata óla ta syngeniká eídi onomázontan Tetigídes í Kikadídes (Cicadidae), apó to ellinikó í to latinikó ichomimitikó ónoma ton tzitzikión.
examples.translation: In older taxonomic systems, all related species were called tettigids or cicadids (Cicadidae), from the Greek or Latin onomatopoeic name for cicadas.

examples.text: Το επιστημονικό όνομα της οικογένειας είναι κικαδίδες και τα πολυάριθμα είδη που περιλαμβάνει ονομάζονται τέττιγες ή τζιτζίκια.
examples.ref: 2022, Παρούτσας, Δ., Κ., “τζίτζικας, ο και τζιτζίκι, το”, in Ετυμολογικό και ερμηνευτικό λεξικό της Ελληνικής Γλώσσας, archived from the original on 28 Apr 2025:
examples.english: The scientific name of the family is Cicadidae and the numerous species it includes are called téttiges or tzitzíkia.
examples.roman: To epistimonikó ónoma tis oikogéneias eínai kikadídes kai ta polyárithma eídi pou perilamvánei onomázontai téttiges í tzitzíkia.
examples.translation: The scientific name of the family is Cicadidae and the numerous species it includes are called téttiges or tzitzíkia.

etymology_text: From translingual Lycaenidae, suffixed with -ίδες (-ídes). Influenced by the family’s etymological cognate, Greek λύκαινα (lýkaina, “she-wolf”).

examples.text: Η Holly blue είναι μικρή πεταλούδα και ανήκει στην οικογένεια Λυκαινίδες (Lycaenidae) και τη συναντάμε μόνο σε ορεινές περιοχές του Τροόδους.
examples.ref: 2011, Μακρής Χριστόδουλος, “Οι πεταλούδες της Κύπρου”, in polignosi, archived from the original on 16 Jan 2025:
examples.english: The Holly blue is a small butterfly belonging to the family Lycaenidae (Lycaenidae) and is found only in mountainous areas of Troodos.
examples.roman: I Holly blue eínai mikrí petaloúda kai aníkei stin oikogéneia Lykainídes (Lycaenidae) kai ti synantáme móno se oreinés periochés tou Troódous.
examples.translation: The Holly blue is a small butterfly belonging to the family Lycaenidae (Lycaenidae) and is found only in mountainous areas of Troodos.

examples.text: Οι κάμπιες των λυκαινιδών ζουν σε συμβίωση με τα μυρμήγκια, ενώ οι κάμπιες μερικών νυκτιιδών είναι σαρκοφάγες και είναι ωφέλιμες γιατί παρασιτούν σε επιβλαβείς κοχενίλες.
examples.ref: 2013, “λεπιδόπτερα”, in Dictionary of Greek, archived from the original on 28 Apr 2025:
examples.english: The caterpillars of lycaenids live in symbiosis with ants, while the caterpillars of some noctuids are carnivorous and are beneficial because they parasitize harmful cochineals.
examples.roman: Oi kámpies ton lykainidón zoun se symvíosi me ta myrmígkia, enó oi kámpies merikón nyktiidón eínai sarkofáges kai eínai ofélimes giatí parasitoún se epivlaveís kocheníles.
examples.translation: The caterpillars of lycaenids live in symbiosis with ants, while the caterpillars of some noctuids are carnivorous and are beneficial because they parasitize harmful cochineals.

examples.text: Η Σούζαν μου μιλούσε για τις οικογένειες που κατοικούσαν στις άλλες αγροικίες, μου έδειχνε τις φωλιές των ασβών και των αλεπούδων, μου εξήγησε τη διαφορά ανάμεσα στις κνιδόκαμπες και τις λυκαινίδες (είδη νυμφαλίδων).
examples.ref: 2022 December 2, Άρης Σφακιανάκης, “«Ταμιευτήρας 13»: Ο Τζον Μακ Γκρέγκορ αναζητά το χαμένο κορίτσι”, in Athens Voice, archived from the original on 28 Apr 2025:
examples.english: Susan told me about the families who lived in the other farmhouses, showed me the nests of badgers and foxes, explained the difference between spiky caterpillars and lycaenids (a type of nymphalid).
examples.roman: I Soúzan mou miloúse gia tis oikogéneies pou katoikoúsan stis álles agroikíes, mou édeichne tis foliés ton asvón kai ton alepoúdon, mou exígise ti diaforá anámesa stis knidókampes kai tis lykainídes (eídi nymfalídon).
examples.translation: Susan told me about the families who lived in the other farmhouses, showed me the nests of badgers and foxes, explained the difference between spiky caterpillars and lycaenids (a type of nymphalid).

examples.text: Παραδείγματα αποτελούν τα ψάρια κοιλάκανθοι (απολιθωμένοι κοιλάκανθοι πιστεύουν οι εξελικτικοί ότι είναι 340 εκατομμυρίων ετών), τα δέντρα Gingko (125 εκατομμυρίων ετών), οι κροκόδειλοι (140 εκατομμυρίων ετών), τα καβούρια Xiphosura (200 εκατομμυρίων ετών), τα βραγχιόποδα Lingula (450 εκατομμυρίων ετών), τα μαλάκια Neopilina (500 εκατομμυρίων ετών) και τα ερπετά tuatara (200 εκατομμυρίων ετών).

etymology_text: Borrowed from translingual Kentrosaurus. By surface analysis, κέντρο (kéntro) + -σαυρος (-savros).

examples.text: Αλλά αυτός ο Κεντρόσαυρος μάλλον δεν πέθανε από καρκίνο των οστών. Αυτός και χιλιάδες άλλοι Κεντρόσαυροι στο κοπάδι του σκοτώθηκαν από μια καταστροφική πλημμύρα, που πιθανότατα προκλήθηκε από μια τροπική καταιγίδα.
examples.ref: 2021 February 23, “Οι δεινόσαυροι έπασχαν από ασθένειες παρόμοιες με αυτές που προσβάλουν τα ζώα σήμερα”, in ΕΡΤ News:
examples.english: But this Centrosaurus probably didn't die of bone cancer. It and thousands of other Centrosauruses in its herd were killed by a catastrophic flood, likely caused by a tropical storm.
examples.roman: Allá aftós o Kentrósavros mállon den péthane apó karkíno ton ostón. Aftós kai chiliádes álloi Kentrósavroi sto kopádi tou skotóthikan apó mia katastrofikí plimmýra, pou pithanótata proklíthike apó mia tropikí kataigída.
examples.translation: But this Centrosaurus probably didn't die of bone cancer. It and thousands of other Centrosauruses in its herd were killed by a catastrophic flood, likely caused by a tropical storm.

examples.text: Αρκετοί σκελετοί Κεντρόσαυρων βρέθηκαν στην Ανατολική Αφρική γύρω στο 1910.
examples.ref: “Δεινόσαυροι”, in Cyprus Museum of Natural History:
examples.english: Several Centrosaurus skeletons were found in East Africa around 1910.
examples.roman: Arketoí skeletoí Kentrósavron vréthikan stin Anatolikí Afrikí gýro sto 1910.
examples.translation: Several Centrosaurus skeletons were found in East Africa around 1910.

examples.text: πήγαινε, προτού γυρίσει σπίτι, στη λιμνούλα την παραπλήσια […]

examples.english: before returning home, [he] would go to the nearby little pond […]

examples.text: […] στον κήπο, στη λιμνούλα και στη σέρα […]

examples.english: […] in the garden, by the little pond and the greenhouse […]
examples.translation: […] in the garden, by the little pond and the greenhouse […]

examples.text: Αριστερά και πίσω ο Εθνικός Κήπος με τα δρομάκια και τις λιμνούλες.
examples.ref: 2000, Γιώργης Γιατρομανωλάκης, Στην κοιλάδα των Αθηνών, Αθήνα: Κέδρος:
examples.english: To the left and behind, the National Garden with its paths and ponds.
examples.roman: Aristerá kai píso o Ethnikós Kípos me ta dromákia kai tis limnoúles.
examples.translation: To the left and behind, the National Garden with its paths and ponds.

examples.text: […] το γλυπτό του Ζογγολόπουλου και δυο λιμνούλες…
examples.ref: 2003 January 24, Χρήστος Μανωλάς, “Το «γιοφύρι» της… Ομόνοιας!”, in ΤΑ ΝΕΑ:
examples.english: […] the sculpture by Zongolopoulos and two ponds…
examples.roman: […] to glyptó tou Zongolópoulou kai dyo limnoúles…
examples.translation: […] the sculpture by Zongolopoulos and two ponds…

examples.text: Χειμώνα, καλοκαίρι, δρόμοι και δρομάκια είχαν μονίμως, από βρωμόνερα, τις λιμνούλες τους και τα ποταμάκια τους.
examples.ref: 1989, Κώστας Μουρσελάς, Βαμμένα Κόκκινα Μαλλιά, Αθήνα: Κέδρος:
examples.english: Winter and summer alike, the streets and alleyways permanently had their puddles and little streams of dirty water.
examples.roman: Cheimóna, kalokaíri, drómoi kai dromákia eíchan monímos, apó vromónera, tis limnoúles tous kai ta potamákia tous.
examples.translation: Winter and summer alike, the streets and alleyways permanently had their puddles and little streams of dirty water.

examples.text: Χιλιάδες χρόνια κλιματικής ιστορίας έλιωσαν και έγιναν λιμνούλα στο πάτωμα […]
examples.ref: 2017 April 11, Βαγγέλης Πρατικάκης, “Μοναδική συλλογή πυρήνων πάγου έλιωσε λόγω βλάβης”, in ΤΟ ΒΗΜΑ:
examples.english: Thousands of years of climate history melted and became a puddle on the floor […]
examples.roman: Chiliádes chrónia klimatikís istorías éliosan kai éginan limnoúla sto pátoma […]
examples.translation: Thousands of years of climate history melted and became a puddle on the floor […]

examples.text: Στο πιάτο, […] σχεδόν πλέουν σε μια λιμνούλα από πράσινο ελαιόλαδο.
examples.ref: 2022 June 10, Άγγελος Ρέντουλας, “Το εστιατόριο στον Νέο Κόσμο όπου θέλουμε να πάμε όλους τους ξένους φίλους μας”, in Γαστρονόμος:
examples.english: On the plate, […] almost float in a pool of green olive oil.
examples.roman: Sto piáto, […] schedón pléoun se mia limnoúla apó prásino elaiólado.
examples.translation: On the plate, […] almost float in a pool of green olive oil.

examples.text: […] με την πρώτη ψιχάλα σχηματίζονται […] λιμνούλες και ποταμάκια.
examples.ref: 2023 October 27, Γιώργος Κώνστας, “Πεζοδρόμιο… σουρωτήρι!”, in Χανιώτικα Νέα:
examples.english: […] with the first drizzle, […] puddles and little streams form.
examples.roman: […] me tin próti psichála schimatízontai […] limnoúles kai potamákia.
examples.translation: […] with the first drizzle, […] puddles and little streams form.

etymology_text: Calque of translingual Corynebacterium, as κορύνη (korýni, “club”) + βακτηρίδιο (vaktirídio, “bacterium”).

examples.text: Το κορυνοβακτηρίδιο της διφθερίτιδας (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) είναι ένα μικρό Gram-θετικό βακτήριο.
examples.ref: 2019 February 11, “Το κορυνοβακτηρίδιο της διφθερίτιδας”, in HealthyLiving.gr:
examples.english: Klebs-Löffler bacillus (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) is a small Gram-positive bacterium.
examples.roman: To korynovaktirídio tis diftherítidas (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) eínai éna mikró Gram-thetikó vaktírio.
examples.translation: Klebs-Löffler bacillus (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) is a small Gram-positive bacterium.

examples.text: Η διφθερίτιδα είναι οξεία λοίμωξη του ανώτερου αναπνευστικού συστήματος που οφείλεται στο κορυνοβακτηρίδιο της διφθερίτιδας.
examples.ref: 2019 November 28, “Διφθερίτιδα: Τι πρέπει να γνωρίζετε για τη σοβαρή λοίμωξη του αναπνευστικού”, in OnMed:
examples.english: Diphtheria is an acute infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by Klebs-Löffler bacillus.
examples.roman: I diftherítida eínai oxeía loímoxi tou anóterou anapnefstikoú systímatos pou ofeíletai sto korynovaktirídio tis diftherítidas.
examples.translation: Diphtheria is an acute infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by Klebs-Löffler bacillus.

etymology_text: From φωτο- (foto-, “light”) + ρύπανση (rýpansi, “pollution”), calque of English light pollution.

examples.text: Η έκθεση στην υπερβολική φωτορύπανση φαίνεται πως επηρεάζει τις πιθανότητες εμφάνισης της νόσου Αλτσχάιμερ για τα άτομα που είναι πάνω από 65 ετών, σύμφωνα με έρευνα στο περιοδικό «Frontiers in Neuroscience».
examples.ref: 2024 September 6, “Αυξημένος κίνδυνος εμφάνισης Αλτσχάιμερ από την υπερβολική φωτορύπανση [Increased risk of Alzheimer's disease from excessive light pollution]”, in newsit.gr, retrieved 31 May 2025:
examples.english: According to a research in the journal Frontiers in Neuroscience, exposure to excessive light pollution appears to affect the chances of developing Alzheimer's disease for people over 65.
examples.roman: I ékthesi stin ypervolikí fotorýpansi faínetai pos epireázei tis pithanótites emfánisis tis nósou Altscháimer gia ta átoma pou eínai páno apó 65 etón, sýmfona me érevna sto periodikó «Frontiers in Neuroscience».
examples.translation: According to a research in the journal Frontiers in Neuroscience, exposure to excessive light pollution appears to affect the chances of developing Alzheimer's disease for people over 65.

etymology_text: ανθρωπό- (anthropó-, “man”) + παύση (páfsi, “pause”). A calque of English anthropause (later also attested as anthropopause), from anthro(po)- + -pause. The term, concerning COVID's impact, was used since 2020; in Greek, by Christos Zerefos, professor of Atmospheric Physics.

examples.text: Αυτή η χρονιά θα μείνει στη σύγχρονη ιστορία ως το πρώτο έτος της Μεγάλης Παύσης ή Ανθρωπόπαυσης (Anthropause), όπως έχει καθιερωθεί πλέον ο όρος.
examples.ref: 2020 December 29, George Stamkos, “2020, το έτος της πρώτης Ανθρωπόπαυσης [2020, the year of the first Anthropause]”, in tvxs.gr, retrieved 25 May 2025:
examples.english: This year will go down in modern history as the first year of the Great Pause or Anthropause as the term is now established.
examples.roman: Aftí i chroniá tha meínei sti sýnchroni istoría os to próto étos tis Megális Páfsis í Anthropópafsis (Anthropause), ópos échei kathierotheí pléon o óros.
examples.translation: This year will go down in modern history as the first year of the Great Pause or Anthropause as the term is now established.

etymology_text: Borrowed from translingual Eucheuma. Equivalent to ευ- (ef-, “good”) + χεύμα (chévma, “pouring”).

examples.text: Τα μεταποιημένα φύκη του γένους Εύχευμα λαμβάνονται από κατεργασία φυσικών στελεχών θαλασσίων φυκών των ειδών Eucheuma cottonii και Eucheuma spinosum της τάξης Rhodophyceae (ερυθροφύκη) με υδατικά διαλύματα αλκαλίων (ΚΟΗ) για την απομάκρυνση των ξένων προσμίξεων, ακολουθούμενη από έκπλυση με καθαρό νερό και ξήρανση, οπότε προκύπτει το τελικό προϊόν.
examples.ref: 2005 January 21, Εφημερις της Κυβερνησεως, 2nd edition, number 67, Ε 407α Μεταποιημενα Φυκη Eucheuma, page 781:
examples.english: Processed seaweeds of the genus Eucheuma are obtained by treating natural strains of marine algae of the species Eucheuma cottonii and Eucheuma spinosum of the order Rhodophyceae (red algae) with aqueous alkali solutions (ΚΟΗ) to remove foreign impurities, followed by washing with clean water and drying, resulting in the final product.
examples.roman: Ta metapoiiména fýki tou génous Éfchevma lamvánontai apó katergasía fysikón stelechón thalassíon fykón ton eidón Eucheuma cottonii kai Eucheuma spinosum tis táxis Rhodophyceae (erythrofýki) me ydatiká dialýmata alkalíon (KOI) gia tin apomákrynsi ton xénon prosmíxeon, akolouthoúmeni apó ékplysi me katharó neró kai xíransi, opóte prokýptei to telikó proïón.
examples.translation: Processed seaweeds of the genus Eucheuma are obtained by treating natural strains of marine algae of the species Eucheuma cottonii and Eucheuma spinosum of the order Rhodophyceae (red algae) with aqueous alkali solutions (ΚΟΗ) to remove foreign impurities, followed by washing with clean water and drying, resulting in the final product.

glosses: Any seaweed or red alga of the genus Eucheuma.

examples.text: Ο ελαίαγνος είναι αειθαλής καλλωπιστικός θάμνος που επιλέγεται συνήθως για το διακοσμητικό φύλλωμά του, αλλά και για τα αρωματικά λευκά μικρά άνθη του.

examples.english: The elaeagnus is an evergreen ornamental shrub that is usually chosen for its decorative foliage, but also for its fragrant white small flowers.

examples.text: Περπατώ στ’ αφρόχειλα της άβυσσος και τρέμω. Δυο φωνές μέσα μου παλεύουν. Ο νους: «Γιατί να χανόμαστε κυνηγώντας το αδύνατο; Μέσα στον ιερό περίβολο των πέντε αιστήσεων χρέος μας ν’ αναγνωρίσουμε τα σύνορα του ανθρώπου.» Μα μια άλλη μέσα μου φωνή, ας την πούμε έχτη δύναμη, ας την πούμε καρδιά, αντιστέκεται και φωνάζει: «Όχι! Όχι! Ποτέ μην αναγνωρίσεις τα σύνορα του ανθρώπου! Να σπας τα σύνορα! Ν’ αρνιέσαι ό,τι θωρούν τα μάτια σου! Να πεθαίνεις και να λες: Θάνατος δεν υπάρχει!».
examples.ref: 1945 [1927], Nikos Kazantzakis, Salvatores dei. Ασκητική [The Saviors of God: Ascesis]:
examples.english: I walk on the edges of the abyss and I am trembling. Two voices inside me struggle. The mind: “Why should we lose ourselves chasing the impossible? Within the sacred enclosure of the five senses, it is our duty to recognize the boundaries of man.” But another voice inside me, let’s call it the sixth power, let’s call it the heart, resists and shouts: “No! No! Never recognize the boundaries of man! Break the boundaries! Deny what your eyes see! Die and say: There is no death!”.
examples.roman: Perpató st’ afrócheila tis ávyssos kai trémo. Dyo fonés mésa mou palévoun. O nous: «Giatí na chanómaste kynigóntas to adýnato? Mésa ston ieró perívolo ton pénte aistíseon chréos mas n’ anagnorísoume ta sýnora tou anthrópou.» Ma mia álli mésa mou foní, as tin poúme échti dýnami, as tin poúme kardiá, antistéketai kai fonázei: «Óchi! Óchi! Poté min anagnoríseis ta sýnora tou anthrópou! Na spas ta sýnora! N’ arniésai ó,ti thoroún ta mátia sou! Na pethaíneis kai na les: Thánatos den ypárchei!».
examples.translation: I walk on the edges of the abyss and I am trembling. Two voices inside me struggle. The mind: “Why should we lose ourselves chasing the impossible? Within the sacred enclosure of the five senses, it is our duty to recognize the boundaries of man.” But another voice inside me, let’s call it the sixth power, let’s call it the heart, resists and shouts: “No! No! Never recognize the boundaries of man! Break the boundaries! Deny what your eyes see! Die and say: There is no death!”.

examples.text: Είναι γεγονός πως όλοι καταγόμαστε από τη θάλασσα και από πλάσματα παρόμοια με τις λάμπραινες.
examples.ref: 2018 July 11, “Το εφιαλτικότερο στόμα της θάλασσας που είναι μακρινός μας… πρόγονος”, in Newsbeast:
examples.english: It is a fact that we all descend from the sea and from creatures similar to lampreys.
examples.roman: Eínai gegonós pos óloi katagómaste apó ti thálassa kai apó plásmata parómoia me tis lámpraines.
examples.translation: It is a fact that we all descend from the sea and from creatures similar to lampreys.

examples.text: Η θαλάσσια λάμπραινα, ανήκει στα πετρομυζοντόμορφα, ένα είδος ψαριού, με κίτρινο-καφέ, στικτό δέρμα, ενώ ο φιδίσιος τρόπος κολύμβησής^([sic]) του το κάνει να μοιάζει με χέλι.
examples.ref: 2024 October 24, Team Pride, “Η διπλή ζωή ενός θαλάσσιου τέρατος”, in Pride.gr:
examples.english: The sea lamprey belongs to the petromyzontiforms, a type of fish, with yellow-brown, spotted skin, while its serpentine swimming style makes it resemble an eel.

etymology_text: Learnedly, from Koine Greek ματαιότης (mataiótēs), based on its accusative singular ματαιότητα (mataiótēta).

examples.text: Ἐπειδὴ τὸ παραπέτασμα μέλλει νὰ πέσῃ καὶ νὰ διαῤῥαγῶσιν αἱ ματαιότητες ὡς πομφόλυγες
examples.ref: 1834, Panagiotis Soutsos, Ο Λέανδρος:
examples.english: Since the curtain is about to fall and the vanities are to burst like bubbles
examples.roman: Epeidí tó parapétasma méllei ná pési kaí ná diarragósin ai mataiótites os pomfólyges
examples.translation: Since the curtain is about to fall and the vanities are to burst like bubbles

examples.text: να πει όσα πίστευε για τη ματαιότητα του πολέμου
examples.ref: 1996 August 4, Karyofyllia Karabeti, quotee, “Η άλλη Ελένη”, in Το Βήμα:
examples.english: to say what he believed about the futility of war
examples.roman: na pei ósa písteve gia ti mataiótita tou polémou
examples.translation: to say what he believed about the futility of war

examples.text: όποιος απόψε άκουσε τον κ. Τσίπρα, γνωρίζει πια τη ματαιότητα κάθε συνεννόησης μαζί του
examples.ref: 2014 October 10, Antonis Samaras, “Συνεδρίαση Ε΄”, in Πρακτικά Βουλής (Hellenic Parliament), page 251:
examples.english: whoever heard Mr Tsipras tonight now knows the futility of any attempt to reach an understanding with him
examples.roman: ópoios apópse ákouse ton k. Tsípra, gnorízei pia ti mataiótita káthe synennóisis mazí tou
examples.translation: whoever heard Mr Tsipras tonight now knows the futility of any attempt to reach an understanding with him

raw_glosses: (formal) futility or vanity; the quality of being pointless, ineffectual, or lacking lasting value
glosses: futility or vanity; the quality of being pointless, ineffectual, or lacking lasting value

etymology_text: From Medieval Greek γηρατειά (gērateiá); the variant γερατειά (gerateiá) is also attested in Medieval Greek.

examples.text: Η καλή υγεία προσθέτει ποιότητα στα γηρατειά.
examples.ref: 2012 April 7, “Παγκόσμια Ημέρα Υγείας”, in Υπουργείο Υγείας:
examples.english: Good health adds quality to old age.
examples.roman: I kalí ygeía prosthétei poiótita sta girateiá.
examples.translation: Good health adds quality to old age.

examples.text: Ο έρωτας ταυτίζεται με τη νεότητα, ενώ ο θάνατος με τα γηρατειά.
examples.ref: 2012, Αρχαία Ελλάδα, ο τόπος και οι άνθρωποι – Ανθολόγιο, ΙΤΥΕ «Διόφαντος», →ISBN:
examples.english: Love is associated with youth, whereas death is associated with old age.
examples.roman: O érotas taftízetai me ti neótita, enó o thánatos me ta girateiá.
examples.translation: Love is associated with youth, whereas death is associated with old age.

glosses: old age; the final period of a person's life, following maturity

examples.text: Στέλνει αυτά τα "περήφανα γηρατειά" στις επιτροπές απορίας...
examples.ref: 2000 December 11, Άγγελος Τζέκης, “Συνεδρίαση ΟΒ΄”, in Πρακτικά Βουλής (Hellenic Parliament):
examples.english: It sends these “proud elderly people” to the indigency committees...
examples.roman: Stélnei aftá ta "perífana girateiá" stis epitropés aporías...
examples.translation: It sends these “proud elderly people” to the indigency committees...

etymology_text: From Medieval Greek γερατειά (gerateiá), through synizesis from earlier γερατεία (gerateía); ultimately based on γῆρας (gêras), with influence from γέρατα (gérata), the plural of γέρας (géras).

examples.text: Και στα πόδια σου να ρίξει κλάψες μύριες, και να δείξει τ’ αχαμνά τα γερατειά του, τη γυναίκα, τα παιδιά του, και του ρούχου τα ξεσκλίδια.
examples.ref: 1826, Διονύσιος Σολωμός, “Το όνειρο”, in Ποιήματα 1823–1833:
examples.english: And to throw himself at your feet with countless tears, and show you his feeble old age, his wife, his children, and the tatters of his clothing.
examples.roman: Kai sta pódia sou na ríxei klápses mýries, kai na deíxei t’ achamná ta gerateiá tou, ti gynaíka, ta paidiá tou, kai tou roúchou ta xesklídia.
examples.translation: And to throw himself at your feet with countless tears, and show you his feeble old age, his wife, his children, and the tatters of his clothing.

examples.text: Τώρα στα γερατειά του γυρεύει νιότα και ζωή, γυρεύει παλικάρια.
examples.ref: 1862, Αριστοτέλης Βαλαωρίτης, “Μνημόσυνον Μάρκου Φλαμπουριάρου”, in Έτερα Ποιήματα:
examples.english: Now, in its old age, it seeks youth and life; it seeks young men.
examples.roman: Tóra sta gerateiá tou gyrévei nióta kai zoḯ, gyrévei palikária.
examples.translation: Now, in its old age, it seeks youth and life; it seeks young men.

examples.text: Κι όμως σαν μπει στο σπίτι του να κρύψει τα χάλια και τα γηρατειά του, μελετά το μερτικό που έχει ακόμη αυτός στα νιάτα.
examples.ref: 1913, Κωνσταντίνος Π. Καβάφης, Πολύ σπανίως:
examples.english: And yet, when he enters his house to conceal his wretched state and his old age, he considers the share he still has in youth.
examples.roman: Ki ómos san bei sto spíti tou na krýpsei ta chália kai ta girateiá tou, meletá to mertikó pou échei akómi aftós sta niáta.
examples.translation: And yet, when he enters his house to conceal his wretched state and his old age, he considers the share he still has in youth.
